source.title: Generalisation First, Memorisation Second? Memorisation Localisation for Natural Language Classification Tasks

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how deliberately introduced label memorization is distributed across layers and how that localization relates to task generalization, refining the generalization-first/memorization-second account. It does not test any listed version's specified outcome.
record.gate_note: The study perturbs 15% of training labels and measures memorization localization. It does not test whether models that fit random labels generalize on natural labels, nor the listed architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, sharpness, or example-removal claims.
record.test_reason: The study localizes deliberately induced label memorization in fine-tuned language classifiers. Its results concern layer involvement and correlations with task generalization, not any V1–V8 outcome. Perturbing 15% of labels does not test V1's comparison between fully random and natural labels, and modifying layers does not test V8's removal of memorized training examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that induced label memorization is gradual, distributed, and task-dependent. Earlier layers are generally more important in the 12-layer models, while middle layers matter most in OPT-1.3B. Later memorization correlates with better task generalization, qualifying the generalization-first, memorization-second hypothesis about processing depth.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes language classifiers after perturbing 15% of training labels, then localizes memorization across layers; it does not use the specified random-label/generalization comparison or interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model affect localization patterns; localization techniques differ, and gradient-based localization is unreliable for Pythia. OPT-1.3B shows a similar task ordering but middle layers are more relevant than late layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Modifying one layer usually causes little memorization error; fully reverting memorization in the OPT RTE and SST-2 case studies requires modifying 7–10 layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For fine-tuned language classifiers with 15% perturbed labels, induced memorization is generally distributed across multiple layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorization-depth measures correlate positively with task generalization measures; pooled Spearman correlations range from 0.54 to 0.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across these language classification tasks, better generalization tends to accompany later-layer involvement in induced label memorization.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The authors state that label flipping is a simplified and potentially unnatural form of memorization; localization techniques are imperfect; centroid analysis is a one-dimensional simplification; and individual examples were not analyzed. Absolute layer relevance values should be treated cautiously.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports extensive per-task, per-model, per-layer figures and appendices, but the supplied text does not provide recoverable numeric values for most individual plotted results. Rows R1–R3 retain the explicit textual summaries and the reported correlation summary.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fully random labels and the corresponding natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy comparison.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce those effects.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against competing measures.
Held-out accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The hypothesis qualified by this study concerns where memorization occurs across layers; it is distinct from V1's coexistence of random-label fitting capacity and natural-label generalization. No verdict on V1–V8 follows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare natural-label and random-label test accuracy or test whether the same recipe fits fixed random labels.
No width sweep or test-error sweep past interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with other generalization-gap measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and measure the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: BERT-base, OPT-125m, Pythia-160m, GPT-Neo-125m
rows.operation_detail: Retrained selected layers using clean examples or swapped in weights from the original-label model; measured error on label-perturbed examples.
rows.value: For most model-dataset combinations, below 15% when modifying one layer.
rows.note: Study-level summary across most, not all, model-dataset combinations; the outcome describes localization, not natural-label test error.
rows.check: The localization result is accurately summarized but cannot establish any listed version. Specify that the value is the maximum error over individual layers for each model–dataset combination. Section 3.1 normalizes memorization error against modifying all 12 layers; that reference should replace the unspecified baseline.

rows.subject: OPT
rows.operation_detail: Swapped layers from the original-label model or retrained selected layers on clean examples.
rows.value: Fully reverting memorisation requires modifying 7 to 10 layers.
rows.note: Reported for both tasks in the OPT case study; modifying only a few layers yielded low error rates.
rows.check: The 7–10-layer summary matches §4.1 but measures reversal of induced noisy-label predictions, not removal of training examples or a change in held-out accuracy. Specify OPT-125m and the normalization reference of modifying all 12 layers.

rows.subject: BERT-base, OPT-125m, Pythia-160m, GPT-Neo-125m
rows.operation_detail: Related task-level measures of memorisation depth to generalization performance.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between memorisation depth and generalization performance
rows.value: Combining data from all models, Spearman's ρ > 0.54; most correlations were stronger per model.
rows.uncertainty: Table 2 reports one correlation with p>0.05; other uncertainty details not stated.
rows.note: The reported association concerns localization depth and task-level generalization measures, not the training-test error gap.
rows.check: The correlation concerns memorization depth, not any listed version's measure. Table 2 gives pooled correlations of 0.54–0.75, so replace ρ > 0.54 with ρ ≥ 0.54. The nonsignificant entry is OPT's M-CoG versus validation score, ρ = 0.52, p > 0.05. Correlation strength does not justify a partial state for V1–V8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
